passage: The phone rang while the pressure cooker whistled, and Zeenat heard her mother say, "Yes, Ma'am... yes, I will speak to her." Dilnaz put the phone down and switched off the stove. Her face was quiet, which was worse than shouting. "The teacher says you called Sana names and left her out of the game." Zeenat's face went hot. "She started it," she began, then stopped, because it was not true. She wanted to slip under the bed. Dilnaz waited. At last Zeenat whispered, "I was mean." They sat on the kitchen floor while the dal cooled, and Dilnaz asked what Zeenat could say to Sana in the morning.

qa.q: What did the teacher say Zeenat did to Sana?
qa.a: The teacher said Zeenat called Sana names and left her out of the game.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat start to say "She started it" and then stop?
qa.a: She felt hot with shame and wanted to blame Sana, but she knew it was not true, so she stopped and owned what she had done.

qa.q: What would be a good way for Zeenat to repair things with Sana?
qa.a: She could say a sincere sorry to Sana without excuses or blame, and ask how to do better, as Dilnaz's question about the morning invites.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz be feeling as she waits in silence?
qa.a: Dilnaz is probably disappointed and worried, yet she stays calm and gives Zeenat room to be honest instead of shouting.

grounding: A child told off after bullying feels hot with shame, resists blaming the victim, and admits it.

passage:
"Gopika, sit down. Your Swati Athai was not always kind, you know. When I was ten, I called a girl in my class 'buffalo' every day because she was bigger than the rest of us.
One evening the teacher came to our house. My mother listened, then looked at me. She didn't shout. She just looked so disappointed. My face burned. I wanted to run and hide. I even said, 'She started it.' That made it worse.
Then I told the truth. The next morning, with Amma beside me, I said sorry to that girl. Amma asked the teacher how I could do better. It was the hardest walk of my life."

qa.q: What name did young Swati call the girl in her class?
What was young Swati feeling when she saw her mother's disappointed face?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, her face burning, and wanted to run and hide.

qa.q: What was the turning point in young Swati's story?
qa.a: When she stopped blaming the girl, told the truth, apologised with her mother beside her, and asked how to do better.

qa.q: How might young Swati's mother have felt when the teacher came?
qa.a: She likely felt disappointed and sad about her daughter's meanness, but calm enough to listen and help her make it right.

grounding: An aunt recalls her mother being told she had been mean; she felt ashamed and blamed the girl, then chose honesty, apologised and asked how to do better.

passage:
The power had gone out, and Nirmala was lighting a candle when the school called. Ramesh heard her side: "Mocking him... every day... I see."
She hung up and sat in the half-dark. "Ramesh. Your teacher says you've been calling Dinesh 'bat-ears' and making the others laugh."
Ramesh's face flamed. "He's always acting weird! He started it!"
Nirmala just looked at him, sad and tired. The candle flickered.
Ramesh's stomach twisted. He looked at the floor. "Okay. I did it. I'm sorry, Amma."
"Tomorrow you say that to Dinesh, not to me. And then we ask your teacher how you can do better."

qa.q: Why was Nirmala lighting a candle?
What was Ramesh feeling when his face flamed?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and defensive, trying to blame Dinesh to hide from what he had done.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Ramesh made excuses and blamed Dinesh, which made it worse; admitting it and agreeing to apologise to Dinesh was the fix.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel hearing about Ramesh's behaviour?
qa.a: Nirmala seems sad, tired and disappointed, but she stays calm and focuses on making it right.

grounding: A mother is told her son has been mean; he feels ashamed and blames the victim, then chooses honesty and agrees to apologise and ask how to do better.
